One might think of modules as agents that are tightly-coupled with high bandwidth and low latency. With existing technology we may be able to build much more capable systems with architectures comprising many modules that function as domain experts, with orchestration and integration using larger, more general modules. 

input --> perceptual pre-processing modules --> relatively general module (routing function) -->  small, narrow domain expert modules --> relatively general module (integration, planning, action function).

comments.author: @TomCraver
comments.text:
One thing that seems impossible to fake, is one's physical presence in a particular place - one can only be in one place at a time.
Verifying that reliably may mean having another randomly chosen human meet one at a randomly generated location and time. 
That way, neither party to the meeting can anticipate who they're going to meet with until they actually meet, so there would be no opportunity to collude in advance so as to NOT be physically present at the meeting, and yet create the illusion of being present, in order to appear to be in two places and thereby be considered to be two different people.
Between 'uniqueness verification' meetings, one could rely on a variety of less secure mechanisms based on that unique identity - a generated cryptokey, continuous location tracking, etc.

comments.author: @phieyl7105
comments.text: TLDW: A study by Tencent suggests that the performance of large language models improves with the number of agents (AI instances) involved, likening it to collective human intelligence where a group's decision-making can surpass an individual's. This concept, referred to as "Society of Minds," demonstrates that more agents working together can produce significantly better outcomes, especially for complex tasks. The study, named "More Agents Is All You Need," utilized a sampling and voting method to demonstrate this effect, where multiple AI agents generate answers and then select the most common one, enhancing accuracy and reliability. The research, conducted with models like LLaMA and GPT-3.5 Turbo across various domains including math and coding, showed a marked improvement in performance as the number of agents increased, particularly notable when moving from one to ten agents. The study underscores the potential of combining this approach with other methods for even greater improvements in AI capabilities. Additionally, it reflects on the broader implications of advanced AI systems in society, discussing challenges like bot-driven click fraud and the need for more secure identification methods in the digital space.

The truth, as it almost always does, will most likely be somewhere in the middle. The grey area. Not the extremes. Life is a bell curve. Extremes are possible but very unlikely. The world in general is far more dull and grey. It’s why we don’t have practically free energy, flying cars or the ability to live as long as we want. 

The future will be different but people need to stop framing it in a binary utopia vs dystopia way as that’s just so very unlikely. But it does grab people’s attention and so those are the narratives that will continue to bubble to the top.
